```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A tariff changes consumer prices and the revenue retained by sellers. This guide
asks how a tariff on one firm's two products changes prices, physical profits and
importing-government revenue. It assumes **trade 0.9.0**, a compatible
**antitrust >= 0.99.43** and **coordination >= 0.1.0** are installed. All inputs
below are illustrative; prices are currency per unit and inside size is units.

## Solve a tariff scenario

`specify()` uses supplied structural parameters. `as_trade_fit()` copies the
fitted game without recalibrating or solving it. `simulate()` solves the policy
change. Firm A owns products a and b, so its choices account for both products.

A producer-value statutory rate `t` becomes the consumer-price fraction
`tau = t / (1 + t)`. Thus a statutory 25% tariff is `.20`, not `.25`, in this API.

```{r tariff-scenario}
library(trade)
source_owner <- setNames(c("A", "A", "B", "C"), c("a", "b", "c", "d"))
source_fit <- antitrust::specify(
  "logit", "bertrand", variant = "standard",
  prices = c(2, 2.2, 2.4, 2.6), ownerPre = unname(source_owner),
  insideSize = 100, labels = c("a", "b", "c", "d"),
  parameters = list(alpha = -1.5, meanval = c(3, 2.5, 2, 1.5))
)
policy_fit <- as_trade_fit(source_fit, tariffPre = 0,
  cost_basis = "effective", margin_basis = "net_revenue")
tau <- .25 / 1.25
scenario <- simulate(policy_fit, tariffPost = c(tau, tau, 0, 0))
pre <- tariff_accounts(scenario, preMerger = TRUE)
post <- tariff_accounts(scenario, preMerger = FALSE)
prices_output <- data.frame(
  product = post$product, firm = unname(source_owner[post$product]),
  canonical_firm = post$firm,
  price_pre = pre$price, price_post = post$price,
  price_change_pct = 100 * (post$price / pre$price - 1),
  q_pre = pre$q, q_post = post$q
)
knitr::kable(prices_output, digits = 3)
```

Read `price_change_pct` as a percentage relative to the stored fitted baseline.
The `q` columns are quantities, not market shares. The original firm labels are
retained by matching product IDs: canonical firm IDs 1/2/3 correspond to A/B/C
in this example. Use the explicit mapping when exporting or joining firm data.
Compare product a, which is
tariffed, with product c, which is untariffed: rivals' prices and quantities can
respond even though their own tariff is zero. These supplied parameters are an
illustrative scenario, not estimates from the displayed price vector.

## Follow the money

Government receives `tau * price * q`; sellers retain `(1-tau) * price * q`.
Physical unit cost excludes the tariff and is measured in currency per output
unit. Multiply it by quantity to obtain total production cost. Net revenue,
producer profit and government revenue are currency totals. Effective unit cost
divides physical unit cost by retention; it is a pricing representation, not
another payment.

```{r tariff-accounts}
product_accounts <- data.frame(product = post$product,
  physical_unit_cost = post$physical_cost,
  physical_total_cost = post$physical_cost * post$q,
  net_revenue = post$net_revenue, producer_profit = post$producer_profit,
  government_revenue = post$government_revenue)
knitr::kable(product_accounts, digits = 3)
account_totals <- function(x) c(
  gross_revenue = sum(x$gross_revenue), net_revenue = sum(x$net_revenue),
  physical_total_cost = sum(x$physical_cost * x$q),
  producer_profit = sum(x$producer_profit),
  government_revenue = sum(x$government_revenue))
knitr::kable(rbind(pre = account_totals(pre), post = account_totals(post)),
             digits = 3)
```

For every product, physical producer profit plus government revenue equals
`(price - physical_cost) * q`. This is an accounting identity over the included
producers, not a finding about national welfare or the nationality of a firm.
The totals table sums all included products: for example, net revenue minus
physical total cost equals producer profit. Government receipts are separate
from net seller revenue.

```{r accounting-check, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(max(abs(post$producer_profit + post$government_revenue -
  (post$price - post$physical_cost) * post$q)) < 1e-8)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(post$price)), all(post$q >= 0),
  max(abs(product_accounts$net_revenue - product_accounts$physical_total_cost -
          product_accounts$producer_profit)) < 1e-8)
```

## Consumer change and margin units

```{r welfare}
welfare <- tariff_welfare(scenario)
fields <- c("physical_producer_surplus_delta",
            "importing_government_revenue_delta", "consumer_variation",
            "monetary_consumer_change")
knitr::kable(data.frame(measure = fields,
  change = unlist(welfare[fields], use.names = FALSE)), digits = 3)
```

The first two entries are monetary changes from the baseline. Positive consumer
variation means compensation required for a price increase; monetary consumer
change is its negative. Producer scope is **all included producers** and
government scope is the **importing government**. Their accounting sum does not
by itself establish a national or exact global welfare measure.

The accounts also distinguish `net_margin`, profit per unit of net seller
revenue; `physical_unit_profit = (1-tau)*price-physical_cost`; and
`effective_unit_markup = price-effective_cost`. These have different units and
cannot be substituted for one another at a nonzero tariff.

## Choose a starting point

| What you have | Operation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Observed inputs and an implemented calibration model | `calibrate()` | Estimate structural parameters from those inputs |
| Supplied structural parameters | `specify()` | Build the specified structural game |
| A compatible fitted game | `as_trade_fit()` | Attach the policy contract without refitting |
| A fitted policy game and a scenario | `simulate()` | Solve the requested counterfactual |

`trade::supportedModels()` lists complete implementations and their supported
operations. Native coordination games are promoted from their own constructors;
their registry entries do not create new trade calibration APIs. Updating inputs,
respecifying a model and simulating a policy have distinct meanings.

## Retention, ownership and limitations

Ownership remains actual ownership; seller retention is separate state. With
uniform retention within each firm, an effective-cost transformation preserves
its optimization problem. Mixed tariffs within a portfolio require the
retained-revenue equations. Multiplying an ownership row by a tariff vector is
not a universal correction, and a tariff alone must not be added again as a
physical `mcDelta` shock.

At a nonzero baseline tariff, effective-cost and net-revenue margin bases must
be compatible with the fitted source; declaring bases cannot repair an
incompatible likelihood or prior. This example holds fitted demand and physical
costs fixed. Calibrated predictions are sensitive to inputs and assumptions;
ordinary deterministic output supplies no automatic sampling uncertainty.

Supported ordinary fitted-game sequential paths can include ownership, cost,
entry and exit changes. Entry is restricted to supported source models. Native
Stackelberg/core-fringe paths require explicit roles after ownership changes and
do not support entry. The explicit `TariffGameFit` route does not handle quotas.

Continue with [a binding quota](quotas.html) ([source](https://github.com/luciu5/trade/blob/master/vignettes/quotas.Rmd)) or
[quantity-setting tariffs](cournot-tariffs.html) ([source](https://github.com/luciu5/trade/blob/master/vignettes/cournot-tariffs.Rmd)). See `?as_trade_fit`,
`?TariffGameFit`, `?tariff_accounts` and `?tariff_welfare` for exact contracts.
The [mathematical reference](https://github.com/luciu5/trade/blob/master/doc/tariff_game_math.md)
retains model theory; [fitted-game reuse](https://github.com/luciu5/trade/blob/master/doc/tariff_game_reuse.md)
covers advanced baseline and posterior conditions.
